title: Shearing a sheep with hand shears
subtitle: Hand shears are slow but quiet, require no power, and suit a small flock where machine shearing is disproportionate.
excerpt: Hand shearing takes 10-20 minutes per sheep for a beginner, down to 4-5 minutes once you have found a rhythm. The sequence follows the same blow pattern as machine shearing: start at the belly, work to the neck, then take the fleece off the back in long blows. The key is keeping the skin stretched taut in front of the blades to prevent second cuts.

glossaryTerms.definition: Spring-loaded scissors designed for sheep shearing, with long blades and a curved handle. Used with one hand, opened against spring tension and allowed to close by relaxing. No motor.

A short piece of wool produced when the shears cut the same area twice, either from incorrect positioning or from trying to even up uneven work. Second cuts lower the value of the wool staple and weaken the yarn.
A lock of wool fibres from a single clip. The length of the staple is the measure from the skin to the tip. A typical UK fleece has a staple length of 5–10 cm after a year's growth.

content.text: Hand shearing is the right tool for a smallholder with fewer than ten sheep who wants to shear on their own schedule without booking a contractor or hiring a machine. The
need to be sharp before you start, blunt blades drag rather than cut, which pulls the skin and distresses the animal. Sharpen on a shearing stone before the session.

Shear after the rise, when the new wool growth pushes a layer of grease up from the skin, separating the old fleece from the new growth. In the UK this is usually late May to mid-June. Running your fingers against the grain, you can feel the break point about 1 cm from the skin where the fleece lifts free. Shearing before the rise produces a fleece that is hard to remove and a sheep that bleeds easily from the cut line.
Sit the sheep on its rump with its back against your legs. Work from the belly first, then the neck, then take the fleece off the back in long blows from the head to the tail.
Belly: clear the belly wool first and discard it separately, belly wool is shorter and dirtier than the main fleece. Use short strokes from the brisket backward.
Neck and head: tip the sheep further back, stretching the neck straight. Shear from the throat down each side of the neck, joining to the belly cut.

Main fleece: begin long blows down the right side from the head toward the tail, keeping the blades flat against the skin. Stretch the skin in front of each blow with your free hand to prevent the skin wrinkling into the blade.

Roll the sheep to the other side and complete the left flank.

Roll the fleece starting from the neck end, folding the edges in and rolling toward the tail. The outside of the fleece faces out; the cut surface is inside. Tie with a strand of the neck wool twisted to a cord rather than with twine, synthetic twine fibres contaminate wool and reduce its value.

attrs.cue: Sheep struggles constantly and will not settle
attrs.cause: Usually positioned incorrectly — sitting too upright rather than resting against the shearer's legs
attrs.fix: Let the sheep's weight come back further against your shins. A properly balanced sheep sits still because it cannot right itself. A sheep that is too upright can twist.

attrs.cause: Wrinkling skin or loose hold while shearing
attrs.fix: Apply wound spray immediately. A small cut heals in 3–5 days. Keep the area dry and check daily for signs of blowfly strike in warm weather.
